why_how.text: A driver arrested for DUI is subject to the implied consent law and is deemed to have consented to the designated breath test for alcohol content, and refusing that test brings revocation of the driving privilege for one year and up to life.

The implied consent law does not mean a fine or jail for having alcohol on the breath, rather it protects a driver who has not been drinking because the test gives a medically accepted measure, and it safeguards the public by arresting those who refuse to be tested.

A DUI or DUI-related event places a revocation on the driving record, and when alcohol was involved the driver may join the Interlock Program, which allows legal driving only in a vehicle fitted with an ignition interlock device that prevents an intoxicated person from starting the car.

Interlock participation is an option for some DUI offenders and mandatory for others depending on the offense, and a driver revoked for two or more DUI or related offenses within a ten-year period must participate.

A driver whose Interlock application is approved before the scheduled revocation begins does not serve a minimum revocation period and can install the device immediately, while a driver who applies late may have to serve the minimum revocation and still complete the program.
Refusing the breath test after a DUI arrest revokes the driving privilege for one year and up to life, a consequence of the implied consent law that is separate from any DUI penalty.

Interlock participation is optional for some offenders but mandatory after two or more DUI revocations within ten years, and applying before the revocation begins is what avoids the minimum revocation period.

why_how.text: Drowsy driving is impaired driving, because after being awake for about eighteen hours driving skills become comparable to those of someone under the influence of drugs or alcohol, reaction time slows and crash risk rises.

A drowsy driver responds more slowly to road and traffic conditions, struggles to process complex information from several places at once, grows careless in driving decisions, has trouble paying attention and may fall asleep at the wheel.

The best way to reduce drowsiness is more sleep, and a drowsy driver should not drive but pull over to a safe area for a short nap, since as little as ten to twenty minutes of sleep can make a big difference.

Drivers should avoid driving at the times they feel sleepy, often early morning, late afternoon or night, and should let a well-rested person drive, carpool, use public transportation, call a taxi or ask a family member or friend to drive.

Another driver may be drowsy when the head nods or drops, the vehicle drifts out of the lane, crosses edge or center lines or hits rumble strips, there are near misses especially rear-end, speed varies erratically with weaving, or the vehicle rear-ends another, hits one head-on or strikes a stationary object.

Signs that you yourself are drowsy include falling asleep at stop lights, yawning, rubbing the eyes, watery eyes, heavy eyelids, not remembering the last few miles, missing road signs or exits, unplanned lane changes, head nodding and driving off the road or onto the rumble strips.
About eighteen hours awake impairs driving like alcohol or drugs, yet a nap of only ten to twenty minutes can make a big difference when drowsiness strikes.

prompt.text: How does drowsiness change a driver's responses?

answer.text: A drowsy driver responds more slowly to road and traffic conditions, struggles to process complex information from several places at once, grows careless in driving decisions, has trouble paying attention and may fall asleep at the wheel.

narration.text: This lesson covers drowsy driving. The handbook sets out these rules. Drowsy driving is impaired driving, because after being awake for about eighteen hours driving skills become comparable to those of someone under the influence of drugs or alcohol, reaction time slows and crash risk rises. A drowsy driver responds more slowly to road and traffic conditions, struggles to process complex information from several places at once, grows careless in driving decisions, has trouble paying attention and may fall asleep at the wheel. The best way to reduce drowsiness is more sleep, and a drowsy driver should not drive but pull over to a safe area for a short nap, since as little as ten to twenty minutes of sleep can make a big difference.

Drivers should avoid driving at the times they feel sleepy, often early morning, late afternoon or night, and should let a well-rested person drive, carpool, use public transportation, call a taxi or ask a family member or friend to drive. The handbook states the following. Another driver may be drowsy when the head nods or drops, the vehicle drifts out of the lane, crosses edge or center lines or hits rumble strips, there are near misses especially rear-end, speed varies erratically with weaving, or the vehicle rear-ends another, hits one head-on or strikes a stationary object. Signs that you yourself are drowsy include falling asleep at stop lights, yawning, rubbing the eyes, watery eyes, heavy eyelids, not remembering the last few miles, missing road signs or exits, unplanned lane changes, head nodding and driving off the road or onto the rumble strips.
